case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a case that was properly removed to federal court on federal-question grounds must be remanded when plaintiffs amend their complaint post-removal to eliminate all federal claims, leaving only state-law claims.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1331 (federal-question jurisdiction) and 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a) (removal); related removal/remand provisions in 28 U.S.C. §§ 1446–1447 and supplemental-jurisdiction principles under 28 U.S.C. § 1367.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that federal jurisdiction in removed cases is determined at the time of removal (the time-of-removal rule) and is not defeated by a plaintiff’s post-removal amendment dropping the federal question. They contend the Eighth Circuit created an atextual, novel exception that allows plaintiffs to divest jurisdiction through strategic pleading changes, undermining the statutory right of removal and conflicting with nearly a century of Supreme Court and lower-court practice. At minimum, once removal was proper, the federal court retains authority to proceed (often via supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state claims) and should not be forced to remand merely because plaintiffs later delete the federal claims.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that when the operative (amended) complaint contains no claim that could support federal jurisdiction, the federal court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction and must remand. They emphasize that "arising under" jurisdiction is assessed by the well-pleaded complaint and the claims actually being pursued; once federal claims are gone, there is no federal-question basis to keep the case in federal court. They frame the Eighth Circuit’s approach as faithful to jurisdictional limits (courts cannot act without jurisdiction), and they resist petitioners’ forum-manipulation framing as a policy concern that cannot expand federal jurisdiction beyond what the complaint supports.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s operative-complaint point is the best response, but it goes to whether continued adjudication is wise, not whether the district court lacked power under § 1447(c) once jurisdiction properly attached at removal. As Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas explain, St. Paul Mercury’s stability principle fits the statutory structure: § 1447(c) targets cases removed without jurisdiction in the first instance, not cases where later amendments eliminate the federal claim. Carnegie-Mellon/Cohill and § 1367(c) provide the narrow, institutionally legitimate off-ramp—broad discretion to remand remaining state claims—without creating an atextual, mandatory-remand rule that would invite manipulation of the removal framework. I would therefore hold jurisdiction does not evaporate, while underscoring that remand will often be the appropriate discretionary course when only state-law claims remain.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 1331 looks to the operative complaint and comity favors sending purely state-law disputes back—does not identify any textual basis in § 1447(c) for mandatory remand when jurisdiction indisputably existed at the time of removal. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Carnegie-Mellon frames the post-dismissal posture as a discretionary supplemental-jurisdiction question, now codified in § 1367(c)’s permissive “may decline,” not a jurisdictional defect. St. Paul Mercury, which Justice Alito and others invoke, reinforces the broader rule that post-removal pleading changes do not divest properly attached jurisdiction; nothing in §§ 1441(a) or 1447(c) makes jurisdiction “evaporate” upon amendment. Under an original public meaning and textualist approach, the Eighth Circuit’s mandatory-remand rule lacks a statutory hook and risks inviting the very manipulation Congress’s removal scheme was designed to prevent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s operative-complaint point does not supply a textual basis for treating post-removal amendments as a jurisdictional defeater under § 1447(c); that provision asks whether the case was removed “without subject matter jurisdiction,” which is fixed at the time of removal under § 1441(a). Justice Thomas’s reliance on St. Paul Mercury is directly on point for the stability principle: plaintiffs may not nullify a properly invoked federal forum by later pleading changes, and nothing in §§ 1446–1447 creates an exception for federal-question cases. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Carnegie-Mellon and § 1367(c) provide ample room for discretionary remand on comity and fairness grounds once the federal claim drops out, without converting that prudential judgment into a mandatory jurisdictional rule that invites forum manipulation. On a textualist approach attentive to practical consequences, the Eighth Circuit’s mandatory-remand rule is both atextual and strategically destabilizing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s invocation of St. Paul Mercury and the time-of-removal principle is the hardest obstacle, and I accept it defeats any theory that the amendment itself automatically “deprives” jurisdiction in the § 1447(c) sense. But that still leaves the core question of what rule should guide the district court once the operative pleading contains no federal claim: as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the proper frame is § 1367(c) and Carnegie-Mellon, and under those standards comity, fairness, and access-to-justice strongly favor remand in the mine-run case. I would not treat this as a mere free-floating discretion that routinely defaults to retention; given the real-world burdens on plaintiffs (especially less-resourced litigants) forced to litigate state-law disputes in federal court, the Cohill factors should create a strong presumption of remand absent exceptional circumstances. So Thomas’s point shifts my rationale away from “jurisdiction vanishes,” but it does not undermine my bottom-line vote that the Eighth Circuit was right to require remand in the ordinary post-federal-claim posture.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that § 1331 looks to the operative well-pleaded complaint, so once the amended complaint drops the federal claim the court no longer has “original” jurisdiction; but as Justice Thomas emphasizes, §§ 1441(a) and 1447(c) frame the jurisdictional inquiry at removal, and St. Paul Mercury’s stability principle fits that structure by rejecting post-removal pleading as a jurisdictional defeater. Carnegie-Mellon/Cohill (as the Chief notes) instead speaks to what the district court should do—often remand—through discretion now codified in § 1367(c)’s “may decline,” not a mandatory § 1447(c) command. I remain persuaded that converting comity and fairness concerns into a jurisdictional divestment rule would be atextual and would invite strategic amendment to nullify Congress’s removal scheme, while robust § 1367(c) discretion addresses the practical burdens Justice Sotomayor highlights.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 1331 follows the operative, amended complaint and that comity favors remand once federal claims vanish—has real force as a matter of sound case management, but it does not supply the statutory hook needed to convert prudence into a jurisdictional command. As Justice Thomas explains by invoking St. Paul Mercury, our cases treat jurisdiction as fixed at the time it properly attaches; §§ 1441(a) and 1447(c) likewise ask whether the action was within original jurisdiction when removed and require remand only when subject-matter jurisdiction was lacking, not when a plaintiff later edits the pleadings. Justice Kagan and the Chief are right that Carnegie-Mellon/Cohill and § 1367(c) channel the comity-and-fairness concerns into a discretionary decision to decline supplemental jurisdiction (including remand), which preserves both federalism values and Congress’s removal framework. A mandatory-remand rule keyed to post-removal amendment would be atextual under these provisions and would invite strategic pleading to defeat removal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument—that federal-question jurisdiction tracks the operative complaint and should disappear once the amended pleading drops the federal claim—still does not fit § 1447(c)’s trigger, which looks to whether the case “was removed improvidently and without jurisdiction” at the time of removal. Justice Thomas’s reliance on St. Paul Mercury is persuasive here: once jurisdiction properly attaches, post-removal amendments ordinarily do not divest the federal court of power; what changes is whether the court should continue exercising supplemental jurisdiction. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Carnegie-Mellon (now reflected in § 1367(c)) supports discretionary remand on comity/fairness/efficiency grounds, not a mandatory, jurisdictional remand rule that would destabilize removal and invite tactical pleading. Institutionally, preserving the time-of-removal rule while underscoring robust § 1367(c) discretion best aligns with precedent, statutory text, and the Court’s interest in predictable jurisdictional rules.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that § 1331 follows the operative well-pleaded complaint, so federal-question jurisdiction should vanish when the federal count is amended away—still does not fit the text of § 1447(c), which makes remand mandatory only when the case was removed “without subject matter jurisdiction,” a determination anchored to the time of removal under § 1441(a). Justice Thomas’s reliance on St. Paul Mercury is persuasive in principle and not meaningfully limited to amount-in-controversy cases: its core holding is that post-removal amendments cannot defeat jurisdiction once properly attached, and nothing in the removal statutes creates a pleading-based divestiture exception. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Carnegie-Mellon properly channels the post-dismissal posture into § 1367(c)’s discretionary declination (and discretionary remand), which addresses comity and fairness without converting prudential considerations into a jurisdictional command. On a textualist/originalist reading, the Eighth Circuit’s mandatory-remand rule lacks a statutory hook and would invite strategic pleading to nullify Congress’s removal framework.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 1331 tracks the operative complaint and that comity/fairness should strongly favor remand once federal claims disappear—persuades me about how district courts should exercise judgment, but it does not convert the situation into a § 1447(c) jurisdictional defect. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the time-of-removal rule preserves properly attached jurisdiction and avoids making removal turn on post-removal pleading tactics, which would undermine procedural fairness and incentivize gamesmanship. Justice Thomas’s invocation of St. Paul Mercury, while arising in a different factual context, reinforces the structural principle that amendments generally do not divest jurisdiction once properly invoked; that principle fits pragmatically here given Congress’s choice in § 1367(c) to make remand/declination discretionary (“may decline”). Under a progressive-pragmatist lens, the right answer is to preserve jurisdictional stability while insisting district courts take seriously Cohill/§ 1367(c) fairness and access-to-justice considerations when deciding whether to remand.

John Roberts.reasoning: Removal jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1441(a) is assessed at the time of removal, and a plaintiff’s post-removal amendment eliminating federal claims should not retroactively defeat that properly attached jurisdiction. Once the federal-question basis drops out, the district court may consider whether to continue with the remaining state-law claims under supplemental jurisdiction principles reflected in 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c), but it is not compelled to remand solely because the amended pleading omits federal claims. Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill recognizes discretionary remand when federal claims are eliminated, not a jurisdictional mandate, and a narrow rule preserving the time-of-removal principle best protects statutory removal rights and institutional predictability while still allowing remand in appropriate cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The removal statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a), authorizes removal of any “civil action” that falls within § 1331, and jurisdiction is assessed at the time of removal; post-removal amendments do not retroactively defeat jurisdiction. St. Paul Mercury Indemnity Co. v. Red Cab Co. squarely states a plaintiff cannot “deprive the district court of jurisdiction” after removal “by amendment of his pleadings,” and nothing in § 1447(c) requires remand where the case was properly removed. Moreover, Congress in § 1367(a)–(c) presupposed continuing adjudicatory authority over related state-law claims even after all claims within original jurisdiction are dismissed, making remand discretionary rather than mandatory. The Eighth Circuit’s mandatory-remand rule lacks textual footing in §§ 1331, 1441, or 1447 and improperly elevates post-removal pleading tactics over the statutory right of removal.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Removal jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1441(a) is determined at the time of removal, and nothing in §§ 1446–1447 creates an atextual rule that a plaintiff can divest federal jurisdiction by later amending away the federal question. The longstanding time-of-filing/time-of-removal principle reflected in Freeport-McMoRan and related cases supports that jurisdiction, once properly attached, is not defeated by post-removal pleading changes. At most, once the federal claims are dismissed, the district court may exercise discretion under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c) (as in Carnegie-Mellon) to remand the remaining state-law claims, but it is not jurisdictionally compelled to do so. A mandatory-remand rule would invite forum manipulation and undermine Congress’s statutory removal right without clear textual authorization.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Federal-question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 depends on the plaintiff’s operative well-pleaded complaint; once plaintiffs amend post-removal to eliminate all federal claims, the federal court no longer has original jurisdiction and should not continue as a matter of course. At that point, any remaining authority would be only supplemental under 28 U.S.C. § 1367, and consistent with Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill the court should presume remand is appropriate where all federal claims have disappeared, particularly to avoid unnecessary federal adjudication of purely state-law disputes and to promote fairness and access to justice for plaintiffs. Nothing in §§ 1441–1447 compels a federal court to retain a case shorn of federal issues, and practical impacts favor returning state-law claims to the state forum best positioned to resolve them. Accordingly, the proper course is remand once the operative complaint contains no federal basis for jurisdiction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Jurisdiction is assessed at the time of removal: if the case was properly removed under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1441(a), a post-removal amendment deleting federal claims does not retroactively eliminate subject-matter jurisdiction, so remand is not compelled by § 1447(c). Under Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill, once the federal claim drops out, the district court generally has discretion—now codified in 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)—to decline supplemental jurisdiction and remand, but that is a workability/administration choice, not a jurisdictional command. Treating the amendment as automatically defeating jurisdiction would create an atextual exception to the time-of-removal rule and invite forum manipulation inconsistent with the removal scheme in §§ 1446–1447. The better reading is: no mandatory remand, but robust discretion to remand under § 1367(c) when only state-law claims remain.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The removal statute looks to whether the case is one "of which the district courts . . . have original jurisdiction" at the time of removal, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1441(a), and our time-of-filing/removal cases reflect that post-removal changes ordinarily do not oust jurisdiction once properly attached. Freeport-McMoRan and related decisions emphasize the stability of jurisdiction once established, and nothing in §§ 1446–1447 makes a plaintiff’s post-removal amendment automatically strip a federal court of power over the case. When the federal claims are later eliminated, the district court may generally choose whether to continue under supplemental jurisdiction or remand under § 1367(c), consistent with Carnegie-Mellon’s recognition of discretionary (not mandatory) remand of the remaining state claims. Treating amendment as a jurisdictional defeater would invite manipulation and contradict the statutory structure distinguishing lack of subject-matter jurisdiction (mandatory remand under § 1447(c)) from discretionary relinquishment of supplemental claims.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Federal-question jurisdiction in a removed case is assessed at the time of removal, and a plaintiff’s post-removal amendment eliminating federal claims does not retroactively defeat that properly-invoked jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1441(a). Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill indicates that after the federal claim drops out, the district court retains power over the remaining state-law claims and may decide whether to remand them as a discretionary matter—now reflected in 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)—rather than being compelled to remand for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. A mandatory-remand rule would invite forum manipulation and undermine the practical workability of the removal regime in §§ 1446–1447, contrary to longstanding practice that post-removal events generally do not divest jurisdiction. The proper approach is to preserve jurisdiction and allow the district court to exercise reasoned discretion to retain or remand the state-law claims under § 1367(c).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The jurisdictional inquiry in a properly removed federal-question case is fixed at the time of removal under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1441(a), and nothing in § 1447(c) requires remand merely because plaintiffs later amend away the federal claim. Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill recognizes that when the federal claim “dropped out of the lawsuit,” the district court retains discretion to remand or retain the remaining state claims—treating the question as one of discretionary supplemental jurisdiction rather than an automatic jurisdictional defect. Congress’s enactment of 28 U.S.C. § 1367 reinforces that understanding by granting supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining “case or controversy,” with § 1367(c) making declination permissive, not mandatory. Accordingly, the Eighth Circuit’s rule compelling remand after post-removal amendment is inconsistent with Cohill’s framework and the statutory text that distinguishes lack of subject-matter jurisdiction from discretionary retention.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: When removal is proper under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1441(a) based on the complaint at the time of removal, a plaintiff’s post-removal amendment eliminating federal claims does not retroactively divest the federal court of subject-matter jurisdiction; instead, the court retains supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state-law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a). Under Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill, once the federal claims “dropped out,” the question becomes one of discretion—guided by § 1367(c) considerations of fairness, comity, and judicial economy—not a mandatory remand for want of jurisdiction under § 1447(c). A mandatory-remand rule would invite forum manipulation and undermine the statutory removal right, while discretion allows district courts to remand where practical consequences and procedural fairness point that way. Accordingly, the Eighth Circuit’s remand-as-jurisdictional approach conflicts with Cohill’s framework and § 1367’s permissive structure.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court loses subject-matter jurisdiction over a properly removed federal-question case when plaintiffs amend their complaint after removal to eliminate all federal claims, requiring remand to state court.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 (federal-question jurisdiction), 1367 (supplemental jurisdiction), 1441 (removal), and 1447(c) (remand for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that jurisdiction is determined at the time of removal, so a case properly removed on federal-question grounds remains within federal jurisdiction even if plaintiffs later amend to drop the federal claims. They contend the Eighth Circuit created an improper exception to the time-of-removal rule by treating a post-removal amendment as retroactively eliminating jurisdiction. Relying on decisions such as Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill, petitioners assert that post-removal deletion of federal claims may affect whether a court should exercise supplemental jurisdiction over remaining state claims, but it does not extinguish Article III/statutory jurisdiction or require remand. They emphasize that the contrary rule enables forum manipulation and undermines defendants’ statutory right to remove.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that when an amended complaint becomes the operative pleading and contains no claims capable of supporting federal jurisdiction, the federal court must remand because it no longer has subject-matter jurisdiction. They frame the question as a straightforward application of the jurisdictional statutes and the well-pleaded complaint approach: if the live complaint does not present a federal question and there is no other jurisdictional basis, the case belongs in state court. They resist an approach that keeps a purely state-law case in federal court based on claims plaintiffs have abandoned, and they dispute that the Court’s precedents compel a rigid time-of-removal rule in these circumstances.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Respondent’s strongest argument—that once the federal claim is amended away the district court “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction” and § 1447(c) mandates remand—still improperly treats a post-removal pleading change as a retroactive jurisdictional defect, destabilizing the time-of-removal rule. Justice Thomas’s textual point is decisive for me: § 1447(c) is triggered only by an actual absence of subject-matter jurisdiction, while § 1367(a) supplies continuing statutory authority over related state claims and § 1367(c) provides the discretionary off-ramp when federal claims disappear. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Carnegie-Mellon and Carlsbad Tech. further supports a narrow, legitimacy-preserving approach: remand here is discretionary and equity-inflected, not jurisdictionally compelled. I would assign an opinion that holds only that jurisdiction does not evaporate upon amendment and that district courts retain broad discretion to remand promptly under § 1367(c)(3), especially when federal claims drop out early.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention—that amending away the federal question makes the district court “lack[] subject matter jurisdiction” under § 1447(c)—fails on the statutes’ text: jurisdiction properly attached at removal under §§ 1331 and 1441, and § 1367(a) then provides continuing supplemental jurisdiction over the related state claims. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, a post-removal pleading change may affect whether the court should exercise that jurisdiction, but it does not retroactively erase adjudicatory power; § 1367(c) supplies the discretionary off-ramp, not § 1447(c)’s mandatory remand rule. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Caterpillar and St. Paul Mercury supports the time-of-removal principle and confirms that later events do not defeat jurisdiction that was proper when invoked. Carnegie-Mellon and Carlsbad Tech., as Justice Sotomayor notes, reinforce that any remand here is best understood as a discretionary supplemental-jurisdiction decision grounded in comity and efficiency, not a jurisdictional defect.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The best argument for Respondent would be that once the federal claim is voluntarily dropped, the federal court no longer has a sufficient jurisdictional basis and § 1447(c) compels remand; but that misreads the statute, which mandates remand only when the court “lacks subject matter jurisdiction,” not when it decides (prudentially) not to exercise it. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the time-of-removal rule fits the text of §§ 1331 and 1441 and avoids converting ordinary post-removal pleading changes into retroactive jurisdictional defeaters. Justice Sotomayor’s focus on practical consequences reinforces that § 1367(c) supplies the proper discretionary framework once the federal anchor drops out, while still preventing plaintiffs from manipulating forum by amendment after a proper removal. None of the opposing theories explains how a voluntary amendment can negate jurisdiction that indisputably existed at removal without collapsing the distinction—central to our precedents—between jurisdictional power and discretionary case management.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that amending away the sole federal claim means the court now “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction” and must remand under § 1447(c)—fails because it treats a post-removal change in the pleadings as retroactively defeating jurisdiction that properly attached at the time of removal. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 1367(a) supplies continuing supplemental jurisdiction over related state claims, and § 1367(c) provides a discretionary, equity-inflected off-ramp; that structure preserves access to justice by allowing remand when fairness and comity so require without turning every amendment into a jurisdictional trap. Carlsbad Tech. reinforces the critical distinction: remands based on declining supplemental jurisdiction are not jurisdictional remands under § 1447(c), so respondent’s theory would collapse a line our cases have been careful to maintain. I also agree with Justice Kagan that Carnegie-Mellon fits comfortably here—not as a mandate to remand, but as guidance for district courts to weigh economy, convenience, fairness, and comity in deciding whether to keep the case after the federal anchor drops out.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that after amendment the court now “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction” and § 1447(c) mandates remand—still misdescribes what changed: the federal anchor claim disappeared, but § 1367(a) continues to supply adjudicatory power over related state claims unless the court declines under § 1367(c). Chief Justice Roberts’s time-of-removal framing preserves statutory coherence between §§ 1331, 1441, 1367, and 1447 by treating post-removal amendments as relevant to discretionary case management, not as retroactive jurisdictional defects. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Carnegie-Mellon and Carlsbad Tech. strengthens the point that remand in this posture is equity-inflected and discretionary, which is hard to reconcile with reading § 1447(c)’s mandatory language to cover situations where jurisdiction once properly attached. On a pragmatic textualist view, respondent’s rule would invite gamesmanship and instability by converting ordinary pleading amendments into jurisdiction-destroying events, effectively collapsing § 1367(c)’s discretion into § 1447(c)’s mandate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that an amended complaint deleting the federal claim means the court now “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction” and § 1447(c) mandates remand—still conflates a jurisdictional defect with a discretionary decision to decline supplemental jurisdiction. As Justice Thomas emphasizes, § 1367(a) provides that district courts “shall have” supplemental jurisdiction over related state claims, and § 1367(c) supplies a discretionary off-ramp once the federal claims are gone; that framework leaves no room to recharacterize the court’s choice as a jurisdictional “lack” triggering § 1447(c). Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on the time-of-removal rule, reinforced by Justice Barrett’s invocation of Caterpillar and St. Paul Mercury, further confirms that post-removal pleading changes do not retroactively defeat properly attached jurisdiction. Carnegie-Mellon and Carlsbad Tech. (as Justice Sotomayor notes) fit comfortably on our side because they treat remand in this posture as discretionary case-management grounded in comity and fairness, not as an automatic jurisdictional command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that amendment eliminating federal claims means the court now “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction” under § 1447(c)—still fails because it treats a post-removal change in claims as a retroactive jurisdictional defect. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, jurisdiction is assessed at removal under §§ 1331 and 1441, and § 1367(a) then supplies continuing statutory authority over the related state claims, with § 1367(c) providing a discretionary off-ramp. Carlsbad Tech. confirms that a decision to remand after declining supplemental jurisdiction is not a § 1447(c) jurisdictional remand, and Carnegie-Mellon frames the inquiry in practical, equity-inflected terms rather than as a mandatory command. Institutionally, this approach preserves the time-of-removal rule, avoids incentivizing forum manipulation, and still leaves district courts ample discretion to remand promptly when comity and efficiency favor state court.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention—that amending away the federal claim means the court now “lacks subject-matter jurisdiction” under § 1447(c)—still fails on the statute’s text and our time-of-removal rule: jurisdiction properly attached under §§ 1331 and 1441 at removal and is not retroactively nullified by later pleading changes. Justice Thomas’s point is decisive for me: § 1447(c) mandates remand only when the court “lacks” subject-matter jurisdiction, while § 1367(a) says the district court “shall have” supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining related state claims, with § 1367(c) supplying a discretionary mechanism to decline it. Carnegie-Mellon and Carlsbad Tech., as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, reinforce that remand after the federal anchor drops out is a discretionary supplemental-jurisdiction decision grounded in comity and efficiency, not a jurisdictional defect. Adopting respondent’s reading would effectively expand § 1447(c) to cover discretionary remands, collapsing the jurisdiction/discretion distinction our precedents and the statutory scheme maintain.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that amending away the lone federal claim means the court now “lacks subject matter jurisdiction” and must remand under § 1447(c)—still fails because it treats a post-removal change in claims as a retroactive jurisdictional defect, contrary to the time-of-removal rule embedded in our cases. Justice Thomas’s statutory point is decisive for me: § 1447(c) is triggered by an actual absence of jurisdiction, while § 1367(a) affirmatively provides continuing supplemental jurisdiction over related state claims, with § 1367(c) supplying the discretionary mechanism to remand on fairness, comity, and efficiency grounds. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on practical consequences and forum-manipulation risk reinforces why we should preserve discretion rather than create a mandatory remand rule that plaintiffs can weaponize through strategic amendment. Nothing in the respondent’s framing explains how jurisdiction that indisputably attached at removal can simply evaporate without collapsing the jurisdiction/discretion distinction recognized in Carlsbad and Cohill.

John Roberts.reasoning: A case properly removed under 28 U.S.C. § 1441 based on federal-question jurisdiction under § 1331 does not lose subject-matter jurisdiction simply because plaintiffs later amend to drop the federal claims; post-removal events ordinarily do not defeat jurisdiction that was proper at the outset. Once the federal claims are gone, the district court’s remaining authority is best understood through 28 U.S.C. § 1367: it retains supplemental jurisdiction over the state claims, but may (and often should) decline it under § 1367(c), considering comity and potential forum manipulation. That framework fits Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill’s instruction that when the federal anchor “drops out,” the question is discretionary remand—not a mandatory remand for lack of jurisdiction under § 1447(c). A narrow ruling preserving the time-of-removal rule while reaffirming district-court discretion to remand under § 1367(c) best protects institutional legitimacy and avoids encouraging strategic pleading.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The jurisdictional statutes, read according to their text, establish that removal was proper because the case initially contained claims within § 1331, and nothing in § 1447(c) authorizes remand merely because plaintiffs later amend away the federal question; remand is required only if the district court "lacks subject matter jurisdiction." After removal, § 1367(a) provides that the district courts "shall have" supplemental jurisdiction over related state-law claims forming the same Article III case or controversy, and § 1367(c) is explicitly discretionary (the court "may decline") when all federal claims have been dismissed. Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill confirms that the post-removal disappearance of federal claims affects discretionary retention of supplemental claims rather than divesting jurisdiction, a principle consistent with the long-settled rule that a plaintiff cannot defeat jurisdiction by post-removal amendment. Accordingly, the district court retains subject-matter jurisdiction and any remand would rest on discretionary supplemental-jurisdiction considerations, not a jurisdictional defect under § 1447(c).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A case properly removed under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1441 does not lose subject-matter jurisdiction merely because plaintiffs later amend to drop the federal claims; § 1447(c) mandates remand only when the district court "lacks subject matter jurisdiction," not when it declines to exercise it. Once the federal claim supplied original jurisdiction at removal, the remaining state claims fall within the court’s supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a), and any decision to send them back is governed by the discretionary factors in § 1367(c), not a jurisdictional defect. Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill confirms that when the federal claim "drops out," the issue is discretionary retention or remand of the pendent/supplemental claims, which also avoids incentivizing forum manipulation after a defendant has properly invoked the statutory right of removal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Jurisdiction in a removed federal-question case is assessed at the time of removal under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1441, and a post-removal amendment dropping federal claims does not retroactively erase that properly attached jurisdiction; instead, it changes what remains for the federal court to hear. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1367, the district court retains supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state-law claims and may, in fairness and with attention to practical impacts, remand those claims as a discretionary matter—often appropriate early in the case—rather than treating remand as mandatory for “lack of subject-matter jurisdiction” under § 1447(c). Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill recognizes exactly that remedial flexibility in removed cases where federal claims drop out, and Carlsbad Tech. confirms that such remands rest on discretion, not a jurisdictional defect. This approach best protects access to justice by allowing prompt remand when federal issues vanish while avoiding rigid rules that invite procedural gamesmanship and waste resources.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Jurisdiction is assessed at removal: if the case was properly removed under 28 U.S.C. § 1441 because the well-pleaded complaint then presented a federal question within § 1331, a post-removal amendment eliminating federal claims does not retroactively divest the district court of subject-matter jurisdiction; it instead alters what remains to be adjudicated. Once the federal claims are gone, the court’s authority over the remaining state claims is governed by supplemental jurisdiction under § 1367, and the question becomes whether to retain those claims or decline under § 1367(c), not whether § 1447(c) mandates remand for lack of jurisdiction. Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill supports this workmanlike distinction by treating post-removal elimination of federal claims as triggering discretionary remand (or dismissal) grounded in comity and efficiency, rather than an automatic jurisdictional defect. A contrary rule would conflate merits/pleading changes with jurisdictional power and invite forum manipulation inconsistent with the coherent operation of §§ 1331, 1367, and 1447.

Once the federal claim that supported § 1331 is gone, what remains is a question of discretion under § 1367(c)—whether to retain or remand the state-law claims—not a jurisdictional imperative to remand under § 1447(c). Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill confirms that in removed cases a federal court may remand state claims after the federal claims drop out, but it frames that decision in terms of prudential factors (economy, convenience, fairness, comity), not as a rule that post-removal amendments retroactively extinguish statutory jurisdiction. Treating post-removal pleading changes as jurisdiction-destroying invites forum manipulation and departs from the ordinary time-of-removal rule embedded in the statutory scheme.

Cohill confirms that in precisely this posture—removed cases where federal claims drop out early—remand is discretionary, not mandatory for lack of jurisdiction under § 1447(c). A contrary rule would invite forum manipulation and undermine the predictable operation of the removal statute by treating later pleadings as jurisdiction-stripping rather than as triggering discretionary supplemental-jurisdiction analysis.
